claim: The official YouTube API does not expose the set of creators on the platform and provides only current, never historical, subscriber counts, which is why population-level creator attrition and survival statistics for YouTube do not exist in the public record.
stance_target: Creator attrition data is structurally unavailable rather than merely unreported
scope_conditions: YouTube platform; as of the paper's writing, May 2026
quoted_support: YouTube does not expose the set of all channels on the platform and does not provide historical subscriber counts (only current values). It also imposes strict daily rate limits.

claim: Social Blade, the most widely cited commercial source of YouTube channel statistics, publicly lists only the top 5,000 channels and retains at most three years of historical metadata, making it unusable for measuring how many creators quit.
stance_target: Commercial creator analytics services can substitute for platform telemetry on attrition
scope_conditions: Social Blade LLC public listings, observed 2008-2026
quoted_support: the firm Social Blade lists only the top 5,000 channels at a given time, and provides historical metadata spanning at most the past three years

claim: Internet Archive captures through end-2023 identify at least 106 million unique YouTube channels across 1.21 billion channel snapshots, giving a lower-bound population denominator for the YouTube creator base.
stance_target: Establishing the size of the YouTube creator population
scope_conditions: Channels ever captured by the Wayback Machine 2006-2023; capture coverage is biased toward larger channels; deduplication across pre-2012 username URLs is incomplete
quoted_support: Format Channel Snapshots Unique Channels Username 372M 34.8M ID 683M 106M Custom 62.4M 5.9M Handle 94.5M 25.4M Total 1.21B At least 106M

claim: A stratified sample of 34,000 YouTube channels observed in October 2025 gives a weighted mean of 46.3 videos per channel, implying 4.39-5.34 billion videos from the census channels, roughly 30-36% of all YouTube videos.
stance_target: Establishing per-channel output volume and census coverage
scope_conditions: Stratified across 17 capture-frequency strata (2,000 channels each); output counts observed October 2025; compared against McGrady et al. 2023 and Zheng/McGrady/Zuckerman 2023 total-video estimates
quoted_support: This yields a mean of 46.3 videos per channel, with a standard error of 2.3 videos (the square root of the variance across strata). Multiplying by 106M known IDs, we form a 95% confidence interval of (4.39, 5.34) billion videos covered.
time_period: October 2025 observation of channels captured through 2023

claim: YouTube channel subscriber growth follows a logistic S-curve that decelerates to an asymptote, implying each channel faces a niche-specific ceiling on audience rather than open-ended growth.
stance_target: Creator audience growth is bounded and plateaus, so income ceilings are structural
scope_conditions: Exploratory analysis of the top 75 most-subscribed channels as of January 2014 only - an extreme survivorship-selected sample; the authors present it as illustrative of what the dataset enables, not as a fitted population model
quoted_support: Each channel exhibits the same pattern of subscriber counts that grows slowly, then quickly, and then eventually approach an asymptote. This suggests that a YouTube channel may capture attention within a niche until it hits a fundamental limit (e.g., total potential audience size)
region: Global; channels observed in English-dominant archive captures

claim: Channels spun off from an already-successful creator skip the slow initial growth phase entirely, meaning existing audience is a substitutable input for the startup period that new creators must otherwise serve out.
stance_target: Time-to-traction for new creators is not a fixed cost but depends on inherited audience
scope_conditions: Qualitative observation from a handful of plotted examples among the top 75 channels of January 2014; no effect size given
quoted_support: In Figure 7, we see that spin-off channels from already successful channels are able to skip the typical initial phase of slow growth.

claim: Median subscriber counts vary by two to four orders of magnitude across content genres among captured YouTube channels, from 53 subscribers for local political campaign channels to 300,000 for South Asian film and music channels.
stance_target: Genre is a first-order determinant of creator audience scale
scope_conditions: 208,893 channels with English-language descriptions of at least 20 characters, drawn from the 577,624 channel IDs captured at least 20 times; heavily upward-biased relative to the full 106M channel population and excludes non-English creators
numbers: local politics n=1,331 median 53 subs / 25 videos / 11,241 views
South Asian film/music n=1,572 median 300,000 subs / 2,086.5 videos
region: English-language channel descriptions only; explicitly excludes non-English Southeast Asian creators
